passage:
At the tenants’ meeting in Porto, the hall clapped for Rafael, who spoke about rising rents in a loud, sure voice. I’m Paulo, and I had come only to hand out flyers, and I felt small.
Then I noticed Marta by the door, printing leaflets and refilling the paper without a word. Ines was writing letters to the council at a side table. Old Joaquim slipped money into the jar for the hall’s hire. Nobody clapped for any of them.
I had been resenting Rafael’s spotlight. Then Rafael turned and said, “Without Marta’s leaflets, nobody would be here.” Marta shrugged, pleased. I picked up my stack of flyers again and stopped counting who got the applause.

qa.q: What was Ines doing at the side table?
qa.a: Ines was writing letters to the council at a side table.

qa.q: Why did Paulo feel resentful of Rafael at first?
qa.a: Paulo felt small handing out flyers while the hall clapped for the loud speaker. Paulo noticed the quiet workers getting no applause.

qa.q: What changed Paulo's view of the work in the hall?
qa.a: Paulo saw Marta, Ines and Joaquim doing quiet jobs the meeting depended on, and heard Rafael name Marta's leaflets. Seeing varied contributions cooled the resentment.

qa.q: How might Marta have felt when Rafael thanked Marta's leaflets in front of everyone?
qa.a: Marta may have felt pleased and quietly proud that the unseen work was noticed. Shrugging and looking pleased suggests public thanks were unfamiliar.

grounding: Shows an observer seeing that a tenants' campaign needs speakers, printers, writers and funders, and how recognition eases resentment.

passage:
The community hall was warm on Sunday, and Mr. Kapoor gave the loudest speech about the school-crossing campaign. I’m Bhavna, and I watched from the third row. Leena, beside me, muttered, “We do the work, and they get the thanks.”
At the back Baljeet sat with a notebook, tallying donation slips and matching them to receipts. Sunita, at the side, was redrafting the petition for the city office.
I said quietly, “Without Baljeet’s accounts, no one would give a rupee. Without Sunita’s draft, the office wouldn’t read it.”
Leena looked around the hall. After the meeting she walked over and thanked Baljeet for the receipts. He looked surprised.

qa.q: What was Baljeet doing at the back of the hall?
qa.a: Baljeet was tallying donation slips and matching them to receipts.

qa.q: Why did Leena mutter that they do the work and others get the thanks?
qa.a: Leena felt overlooked and resentful, since the loud speeches got the attention while the quiet work went unnoticed.

qa.q: What did Bhavna's remark change for Leena?
qa.a: Bhavna pointed out how Baljeet's accounts and Sunita's draft made the campaign possible. Leena then looked around the hall and thanked Baljeet.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt when Leena thanked him?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and pleased, since he looked surprised. Nobody had thanked him for the receipts before.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing that a campaign needs speakers, accountants and writers alike, and that recognising each role reduces resentment.
